why: The ad business is genuinely strong. Revenue grew 28% and both ad pricing and ad volume grew double digits — growth is not the question here.

But the profit and the cash did not follow it. Operating income fell 8%, free cash flow collapsed 91% to $784M, and Family of Apps — the segment that actually earns the money — saw its own operating income shrink 6%.
The balance sheet is doing a lot of the work. Meta raised $55B of new bonds in nine months and is now guaranteeing up to $13B on a data-center joint venture it just moved off its own books.

The tax line is not settled. Two one-time items swung diluted EPS from $1.05 to $10.44 in two quarters, and a live IRS notice puts another $15.89B on the table — on a transfer-pricing argument Meta already lost once in Tax Court.

The price is not the argument against this stock. At {price|$} you are already just below my base case of {fair.base|$}, and well below the {fair.bull|$} the AI bull case would require. What I am watching is not the tape — it is whether the tax dispute, the debt-funded buildout and the shrinking segment margin resolve.

notes.findings: Meta just posted twenty-eight percent revenue growth and the stock barely moved on it. That headline is true and it is not the story. I read the ten-Q behind it, and here are four things that are in the filing and not in the press release. Each one changes how you should read this quarter, and we're going to take them one at a time. TARGET 26s.
notes.quarter: First, the quarter as they reported it. Revenue sixty point eight billion, up twenty-eight percent — genuinely strong. But operating income actually fell, margin went from forty-three percent to thirty-one, and free cash flow — the cash left over after the business runs itself — nearly vanished. That gap between the top line and everything below it is the whole episode. TARGET 28s.
notes.taxwhiplash: Here's why the earnings number is so hard to trust right now. Third quarter last year, a fifteen point nine billion dollar one-time tax charge crushed EPS down to a dollar oh five — it would have been seven twenty-five without it. Two quarters later, an eight billion dollar one-time tax benefit did the opposite, pushing EPS up to ten forty-four. Same company, same underlying business, ten dollars of reported earnings per share apart. Neither number was really about the business. TARGET 28s.
notes.irs: And that's not the end of it — it's the preview. Buried in the tax note: the IRS is now asking for another fifteen point nine billion dollars for 2017 through 2019, on the exact transfer-pricing argument Meta already fought and partially lost in Tax Court last year. This isn't hypothetical risk language. It's a number, on a fight they've already lost once. TARGET 26s.
notes.foa: Now the finding that matters most for what this company is actually worth. Family of Apps — the ads business, the thing that pays for everything else — grew revenue nicely. Its operating income went the other way. Look at the two bars: revenue climbing, profit falling, same segment, same quarter. Legal costs and infrastructure spend landed inside the one business that is supposed to be the cash machine. TARGET 26s.
notes.capexpath: Why is infrastructure eating the profit engine? Because the capital spending plan for this year has been revised upward at every single release — never once cut, never once held flat. It started the year at a range topping out around a hundred thirty-five billion and now sits even higher. This is not a company trimming its ambitions. TARGET 24s.
notes.debt: And here's how that spending actually gets paid for. Two bond sales, six months apart, twenty-five billion dollars or more each — bigger, combined, than every dollar of debt Meta had issued in its entire history before that. The interest bill on those bonds more than tripled year over year in a single quarter. The AI buildout is being financed, not just funded out of cash flow. TARGET 26s.
notes.offbalance: And some of it isn't even on the balance sheet yet. In July, Meta agreed to hand a data center over to a joint venture for a twenty percent stake and a quick billion-dollar payout — while guaranteeing up to thirteen billion dollars if that venture falls short. Add in the leases that haven't even started and the non-cancelable commitments sitting in the footnotes, and there's a lot more building than the balance sheet shows today. TARGET 26s.
notes.insiders: What are the people running the company doing with their own money? Selling — nobody's buying on the open market. It's real money, a few hundred million dollars worth. To be fair, almost all of it runs through pre-scheduled trading plans set up months in advance, so don't read too much timing into it. But zero purchases, at any price, from anyone, is still zero. TARGET 22s.
notes.peers: So what are you actually paying for all of this? I've put Meta next to the other mega-cap names on the same basis — price against next year's expected earnings, growth rate right beside it, because cheap and cheap-for-its-growth are different claims. Meta isn't the most expensive name on this list, and it isn't the cheapest either — it's paying a normal multiple for above-average growth, which is a fine place to be if the profit line stabilizes. TARGET 24s.
notes.street: Before my own call, here's what Wall Street's models actually say. Most analysts still rate this a buy, and the average target sits well above today's price. But look at what's happening underneath: more analysts are cutting their earnings estimates than raising them, even with the stock this close to its highs. The professionals are optimistic on the target and getting quietly less optimistic on the earnings that are supposed to get it there. TARGET 24s.
notes.call: So here's the whole thing on one ruler. My model's range runs from a bear case down here to a bull case up there, with today's price sitting just below my base case — not expensive, not a screaming bargain either. My call is WATCH. The growth is real. The fine print — the tax whiplash, the unresolved IRS fight, the debt-funded buildout, a chunk of it moving off the balance sheet — is also real, and it's exactly why the market isn't paying up for the headline number the way you'd expect. That's the fundamentals. Now let's go to the chart. TARGET 30s.
